newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Mining companies eye Zaire's riches greedily.
newsitem.headline: Mining companies eye Zaire's riches greedily.

text.p: As Laurent Kabila's troops conquer more of Zaire, mining companies from all over the world discover a fresh interest in the rebel cause.

Dealers in the world's biggest diamond trading centre in Antwerp greedily eye new business opportunities since Kabila's soldiers have taken over the provinces of Shaba and Kasai - areas of the world so unbelievably rich in minerals that experts speak of a geological scandal.

"People with mining concessions and interests are talking with Kabila", Marcel Pruwer, an Antwerp-based diamond broker with the Canadian company Rex Diamond Mining Corp, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"New people will be trying to get in," he added. "But none of the companies already active will let go very easily. They know very well how to move very quickly."

Diamonds are Zaire's biggest foreign currency earner. Most of the stones mined in the Central African country don't have the size or the quality needed for jewelry, but they can be used for industrial purposes -- for instance as drilling bits.
By weight one sixth of last year's world production of diamonds came from Zaire. By value industry sources put the figure at around $450 million, not taking into account illicit diamond mining.

For Kabila, possession of the diamond mines has become a double asset: he has cut off embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko from his mining income and he has been able to keep the mines running for the benefit of his own movement.
Diamond industry sources in Belgium tell the story of how careful Kabila has been not to disrupt the mining operations.

When Kabila's troops conquered the diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi in early April, Kabila posted soldiers around the mining operations of Societe Miniere the Bakwanga (Miba) to stop looting, one industry source said.
"There was a bit of confusion for a few days, a little bit of damage done, a few cars disappeared," the source said. "But overall Miba continued almost as normal."
Miba is the largest and most modern diamond mine in Zaire. Eighty percent of the company belong to the Zairean state, the other 20 percent are owned by Belgium's Sibeka.
Sibeka's parent company, Union Miniere, already exploited mines in Zaire when the country was still a Belgian colony by the name of Congo.

Today the world's biggest diamond company, South Africa's De Beers, owns a stake in Sibeka and has the right to sell all of Miba's diamonds through its marketing cartel, the Central Selling Organisation (CSO), in London.
But Kabila has been eager to establish good contacts with other mining companies as well.
"We are now in contact with all the companies who have concessions here and other companies who are interested in coming here as well," Kabila told Reuters in an interview as early as January.
"My soldiers have been given special instruction to keep the mines in good condition," he added.

Miba produces only a fourth of Zaire's yearly diamond harvest, with the majority of the stones coming from small- scale operations, according to a report in the specialist publication Diamond International.
These independent operations influence CSO prices in London and therefore the world market, Antwerp broker Pruwer said.

If Kabila replaces Mobutu's regime with a functioning administration, Zaire could become an even more important source of minerals, Pruwer added. Mining specialists for diamonds, copper, cobalt, zinc and gold would be willing to risk much higher investments.
"If Kabila makes the right noises, you'll see planes full of blue chip executives on their way to Zaire," Pruwer said.
